decks.domain: Towing with a Class C license: limits, loading, hitching, inspection, backing, turning, clearance and combination vehicles

cards.front: What may a non-commercial Class C driver tow, by weight rating and length?
cards.back: A non-commercial Class C driver may tow a single vehicle or a combination as long as its gross vehicle weight rating does not exceed 10,000 pounds and the whole unit is seventy feet long or shorter.
cards.memory_hook: Class C: weight and length caps

cards.front: Where can you learn more about towing or the J endorsement?
cards.back: Drivers who want more towing information, or a J endorsement, should read the Nevada Non-Commercial A and B, J Endorsement Study Guide on the DMV website.

cards.front: What is the difference between gross vehicle weight and gross combination weight?
cards.back: Gross vehicle weight is the total weight of one vehicle plus its load, while gross combination weight is the total of the powered unit, its trailer or trailers, and the load.

cards.front: What is the gross combination weight rating?
cards.back: Gross combination weight rating is the manufacturer's stated combined loaded weight for a vehicle and the vehicle it tows.

cards.front: How does gross combination weight differ from gross combination weight rating?
cards.back: Gross combination weight is what the rig and load actually weigh, while the gross combination weight rating is the maximum combined loaded weight the manufacturer specifies.

cards.front: What is axle weight?
cards.back: Axle weight is the weight one axle or one set of axles puts on the ground.

cards.front: What does a tire's load rating tell you, and what else carries a rating?
cards.back: A tire's load rating, printed on its sidewall, is the most weight it can carry safely at a stated pressure; suspensions and coupling devices also carry maximum weight ratings.

cards.front: Why is loading a trailer wrongly dangerous?
cards.back: Loading a trailer wrongly endangers you and others, since loose items can strike other road users and a quick stop or crash can damage the trailer's interior.

cards.front: How does overloading affect a towing rig?
cards.back: Overloading hurts steering, braking and speed control: an overloaded rig crawls up hills, gains too much speed downhill, needs longer to stop, and its overworked brakes can fail.

cards.front: How should you load cargo to avoid overturning?
cards.back: The higher a load's center of gravity, the more likely the vehicle is to overturn, so keep cargo as low as possible and put the heaviest items underneath or in lower compartments.

cards.front: What happens with too much or too little weight on the steering axle?
cards.back: Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard and can damage that axle and its tires, while too little weight up front can leave the steering axle too light to steer safely.

cards.front: What happens with too little weight on the driving axles?
cards.back: Too little weight on the driving axles gives poor traction and lets the drive wheels spin easily.

cards.front: How does uneven side-to-side loading affect a trailer, and how do you prevent rollovers?
cards.back: Uneven side-to-side loading can tip a trailer over, especially in turns; to prevent a rollover, take turns slowly and keep cargo close to the ground.

cards.front: What extra risks come with flatbed trailers and bad weather?
cards.back: Flatbed trailers carry a greater risk of the load shifting sideways or falling off, and in bad weather a poorly balanced rig may not stay balanced.

cards.front: What should you check about the load and doors before a trip?
cards.back: Pre-trip, make sure the load is balanced and secured and every outside storage compartment door is latched or locked.

cards.front: What does a load-distributing hitch do, and when is it used?
cards.back: A load-distributing hitch spreads the tongue load across all axles of the tow vehicle and trailer to steady the tow vehicle, and is used for heavier utility, boat and travel trailers.

cards.front: What must you check when hitching a ball coupler?
cards.back: When hitching a ball coupler, the ball must be seated firmly in the coupler, the coupler safety latch secured down, and the safety chains attached and crossed.

cards.front: How must the ball mount and electric lines be secured?
cards.back: The ball mount must be locked into the tow vehicle's receiver with its pin and clip or other locking device, and the electric lines must be seated, locked and free of tangles or dragging.

cards.front: What should you confirm about the coupling parts and tongue before towing?
cards.back: Before towing with a ball hitch, confirm every coupling part is present and unbroken and the trailer tongue is not bent, cracked or damaged.

cards.front: How do a ball-and-hitch coupler and a fifth-wheel hitch differ?
cards.back: A ball-and-hitch coupler joins a ball on the tow vehicle to a coupler on the trailer tongue, whereas a fifth-wheel hitch sits in a truck bed and locks onto a kingpin and is less prone to balance problems.

cards.front: What is a fifth-wheel hitch, and what is its drawback?
cards.back: A fifth-wheel hitch mounts in a pickup bed and couples to the trailer's kingpin; it is very stable but uses most of the bed and needs the space behind it kept clear for turns.

cards.front: What must you do before and after coupling a fifth wheel?
cards.back: Before backing under a fifth-wheel trailer, lock the trailer brakes, and after the jaws close around the kingpin, make sure the locking lever is locked or the coupling is not properly seated.

cards.front: What should you check on the fifth-wheel mount and kingpin?
cards.back: Check that the fifth-wheel mounting assembly is solidly attached with no loose or missing parts and that the kingpin is not bent.

cards.front: What must a coupled fifth wheel look like?
cards.back: A coupled fifth wheel must have no gap between the upper and lower coupling, the trailer must sit flat on the skid plate, and the plate must be greased as required.

cards.front: What must you check on fifth-wheel lines, platform and release arm?
cards.back: Fifth-wheel electric lines must not be chafed, spliced or worn, the platform supporting the skid plate must be free of cracks, and the release arm must be engaged with any safety latch in place.

cards.front: How do you test a hitch before driving?
cards.back: Test the hitch by pulling gently forward in low gear against the locked trailer brakes, then look at the connection; chains and electric lines should be secure with enough slack for turns.

cards.front: When should you re-inspect the trailer on a long trip?
cards.back: On a long trip, re-inspect the trailer and its load-securing devices within the first fifty miles, then again after three hours or one hundred fifty miles of driving, and ideally at every break.

decks.domain: Towing with a Class C license: limits, loading, hitching, inspection, backing, turning, clearance and combination vehicles

cards.front: Is signalling while towing required?
cards.back: Signalling your intentions while towing is required by law as well as being important for safety.

cards.front: What is a major cause of crashes, and how do you counter it while towing?
cards.back: A lack of awareness is a major cause of crashes, so use your mirrors often, signal, and make other drivers aware of your vehicle even when it is in plain sight.

cards.front: Why do empty trucks need longer to stop than loaded ones?
cards.back: Empty trucks actually need longer stopping distances than loaded ones, because they have less traction and can bounce and lock their wheels.

cards.front: How does vehicle weight affect the brakes?
cards.back: A heavier vehicle makes the brakes work harder and absorb more heat, yet heavy-vehicle brakes, tires, springs and shocks work best when fully loaded.

cards.front: Why does managing space matter more with a towing rig?
cards.back: Large vehicles take up more space and need more room to stop and turn, so managing the space around a towing rig matters even more than in a car.

cards.front: How do you steer when backing a trailer compared with a single vehicle?
cards.back: When backing a single vehicle you turn the top of the steering wheel toward where you want to go, but when backing a trailer you turn it the opposite way, then follow the trailer once it starts turning.

cards.front: How does backing a car differ from backing a trailer?
cards.back: Backing a car, turn the top of the wheel toward where you want to go; backing a trailer, turn it the opposite way at first and then follow the trailer.

cards.front: How can you avoid backing when towing?
cards.back: Backing is always dangerous, so avoid it when you can, and park so you can pull forward when leaving.

cards.front: What should you do before backing a trailer?
cards.back: Before backing a trailer, get out and walk around to check your path and clearance to the sides and overhead, then back as slowly as possible.

cards.front: What should you look for overhead before backing into an area?
cards.back: Before backing into an area, get out and look for overhanging trees, branches or electric wires, which are easy to miss while reversing.

cards.front: How do you correct a trailer drifting while backing?
cards.back: If the trailer starts drifting off course while backing, correct at once by turning the top of the steering wheel toward the drift.

cards.front: Which way should you back and turn when possible, and why?
cards.back: Back and turn toward the driver's side whenever possible, even if it means circling the block, because backing toward the right side is very dangerous.

cards.front: How should a helper guide you while backing?
cards.back: Use a helper standing near the rear where you can see them, and agree on hand signals, including one for stop, before you begin backing.

cards.front: What helps when backing a trailer along a path?
cards.back: While backing a trailer, try to set up a straight-line path, watch the mirrors for drift, and pull forward to reposition whenever needed.

cards.front: How do you make a tight right turn with a trailer?
cards.back: On a right turn that needs extra room, turn wide only as you finish the turn and keep the trailer's rear near the curb; do not swing wide left at the start, which invites drivers to pass on your right.

cards.front: What should you do if you must cross into oncoming traffic to turn?
cards.back: If you must cross into oncoming traffic to turn, give oncoming vehicles room to pass or stop, but do not back up for them.

cards.front: When should you start a left turn with a trailer?
cards.back: On a left turn with a trailer, reach the center of the intersection before turning, because turning early lets off-tracking swing the vehicle's left side into other traffic.

cards.front: Which lane should you use when there are two left-turn lanes?
cards.back: With two left-turn lanes, always use the right-hand one, since starting from the inside lane may force you to swing right into drivers you cannot see.

cards.front: What goes wrong when turning left too early or from the inside lane?
cards.back: Turning left too early lets off-tracking carry your left side into vehicles beside you, while starting from the inner of two left-turn lanes risks swinging right into drivers you cannot see.

cards.front: Why does a towing rig need a bigger gap to cross or enter traffic?
cards.back: A towing rig accelerates slowly, so it needs a much bigger gap to cross or enter traffic, more so when heavily loaded; be sure you can clear the road before traffic arrives.

cards.front: Why shouldn't you trust posted bridge heights?
cards.back: Do not trust posted heights at bridges and overpasses, since repaving or packed snow may have lowered the clearance, and an empty trailer rides higher than a loaded one.

cards.front: What should you do if you doubt you can fit under an object?
cards.back: If you doubt you can fit under an object, go slowly, and if still unsure, take another route; low bridges may not be marked.

cards.front: What should you do where the road tilts toward roadside objects?
cards.back: Roads that tilt a vehicle can bring it into signs or trees at the edge, so where that is a risk drive a little closer to the center of the road.

cards.front: Why cross raised tracks and drainage channels carefully when loaded?
cards.back: Heavily loaded vehicles have little ground clearance, so cross raised railroad tracks and drainage channels carefully to avoid getting hung up or dragging.

decks.domain: Towing with a Class C license: limits, loading, hitching, inspection, backing, turning, clearance and combination vehicles

cards.front: Which towed vehicle goes first in a combination?
cards.back: In a combination of towed vehicles, the heaviest vehicle must always be placed first behind the towing vehicle, with the lighter one at the rear.

cards.front: How do combination vehicles differ from single vehicles?
cards.back: Combinations of vehicles are heavier and longer than single vehicles, need more driving skill, and have been involved in many crashes where only the trailer overturned.

cards.front: What is the crack-the-whip effect, and how do you avoid it?
cards.back: Trailers have a crack-the-whip effect, caused by rearward amplification and worse with more trailers, which can flip a trailer during a quick lane change, so steer gently and smoothly.

cards.front: What do the rearward amplification values mean?
cards.back: In the rearward amplification chart, a value of two point zero means the rear trailer is twice as likely to overturn as the truck, and triples reach three point five.

cards.front: Why do empty combination rigs take longer to stop?
cards.back: Empty combination rigs take longer to stop than loaded ones because stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction, so allow long following distances and look far ahead to brake early.

cards.front: When is a trailer jackknife more likely, and how do you spot it early?
cards.back: A trailer jackknife is more likely when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded; spot it early in the mirrors whenever you brake hard, because once the trailer leaves the lane a jackknife is very hard to stop.

cards.front: How do you recover when the trailer wheels lock and skid?
cards.back: If trailer wheels lock and the trailer starts to skid, release the brakes to regain traction, and do not use the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig, since trailer braking caused the skid.

recap_hooks.text: Class C may tow within a set weight rating and a seventy-foot length; the J endorsement guide covers heavier towing.
Combination weight is what the rig weighs, while the rating is the maker's maximum.
Keep cargo low and the heaviest items underneath, and balance it front to back and side to side.
Seat the ball, latch the coupler and cross the chains, and lock the fifth-wheel lever after the jaws close.
Re-inspect within the first fifty miles, then after three hours or one hundred fifty miles.
Backing a trailer, turn the top of the wheel the opposite way, then follow the trailer, and back toward the driver's side.
Empty trucks need longer to stop than loaded ones.
Turn wide only at the end of a right turn, and reach the middle of the intersection before turning left.
Do not trust posted bridge heights, and reroute if unsure.
Put the heaviest towed vehicle first, and steer gently to avoid the crack-the-whip effect.
If the trailer skids, release the brakes and never use the trailer hand brake to straighten it.
